title: Slack Water
bodyMd:
**Literary narrative.** This passage is adapted from an original short story.

The tide clock in my grandmother’s kitchen had two hands and no numbers, and for the first eleven summers of my life I believed it was broken. It never agreed with the clock on the stove. Nan would glance at it while she was drying a plate and say, “Two hours yet,” and two hours later the mudflats behind the house would be gone under water, and I would still not understand what she had read.

She ran the crossing at Ardvane — a flat-bottomed boat, eight passengers, a rope strung between two posts, and a schedule that nobody printed because it changed every day. The mainland bus company had asked her twice for fixed departure times so that their timetable could show a connection. Twice she had written back that the sea did not take instruction, and twice they had sent the same letter again the following spring.

The summer I turned twelve she began letting me work the rope. She never taught me anything directly. She would simply stop doing a thing, and wait, and I would eventually do it badly, and she would let me. When I hauled us in too fast and cracked the gunwale against the jetty, she said only, “You will remember that.” I did.

What I could not learn was the clock. I could see the water; I could not see the hour in it. Then one August evening, waiting out a squall with the boat tied and nothing to do, I watched the flats for an hour and a half and saw the moment when the water stopped. It did not turn. It simply held — no run in it, no direction, the whole channel gone flat and slow as poured glass. Nan came out with two mugs and did not ask what I was looking at.

“Slack water,” she said. “Nothing to fight for twenty minutes. Best time to cross, and the only time nobody believes you.”

I went inside and looked at the two hands on the kitchen wall and found, for the first time, that I already knew what they would say.
accessibilityText: A first-person literary narrative of six short paragraphs. The narrator recalls childhood summers at a grandmother’s house beside a tidal channel. The grandmother, called Nan, operates a small rope-guided ferry at a place called Ardvane and reads the tide from a numberless two-handed tide clock in her kitchen. The narrator describes being unable to understand the clock, being taught to work the ferry rope by being left to make mistakes, and finally watching the channel go still at slack water and realising the clock had become readable. All names, places and details are invented.

provenance.notes: Original prose-fiction passage written for this bank. Ardvane, Nan, the tide clock and every incident are invented; nothing here is drawn from, or modelled on, any published ACT Reading passage or any existing literary work.
